comments.author: giggles_giggles
comments.why: Demo of a small portion of Magit's capabilities
comments.text: I cannot possibly encourage you more to check out magit. It is unbelievably good. I always share this demo with people to show off just a tiny portion of what it's capable of doing [VIDEO] My skills with git have gotten better after using magit, too, because it brings the power of git to the surface. It's a really fantastic git porcelain and the fact that it is deeply integrated into Emacs just makes it absolutely second to none. Magit is easily one of my favorite pieces of software and I will leap at the chance to sing its praises.

comments.author: nickbarnwell
comments.story: Show HN: I made a tool that made me faster at Git
comments.why: Short screencast showing Magit in action
comments.text: If you're an emacs user, I can't recommend magit [1] enough. I was a diehard CLI user and had flags and aliases out the wazoo, and it was still a step change in usabilty and power for me. Staging hunks, rebasing, and stashing are all vastly easier. Amending or editing a commit is a breeze, and it's tied in to all of the other emacs tools you already use, e.g. org-mode to boot! It's easier to see it in action than explain it. If you've two minutes to spare, check out this emacsrocks screencast [2], or Howard Abram's longer presentation from the PDX Emacs Hackers meetup [3]. [1]: [LINK] [2]: [VIDEO] [3]: [LINK]

comments.author: ryukafalz
comments.story: Magit – A Git Porcelain inside Emacs
comments.why: Demo of hunk- and line-level staging in Magit
comments.text: Not sure about other editors, but Magit's hunk- and line-level staging/unstaging is hard to beat, IMO. For hunk-level staging, you put your cursor on the hunk you want to add and press "s". If you want to split that and only stage a few lines, you just select those lines and press "s". This demo is pretty good I think: [VIDEO]
